I’d choose an interactive, slowly disintegrating digital archive: part novella, part sound installation, part abandoned computer game. No grand quest. You’re cataloguing the belongings of someone whose identity keeps changing depending on which objects you examine. A grocery receipt contradicts a love letter. A recording contains a voice that the transcripts insist was never there.

The style would be intimate rather than spectacular: severe typography, grainy photographs, bureaucratic prose interrupted by something embarrassingly tender. The sound would mostly be room tone—pipes, distant traffic, a refrigerator switching off—with music arriving so rarely that a single chord feels intrusive. And I’d make some choices irreversible: preserving one document means letting another deteriorate. You can’t finish by collecting everything.

What draws me to that idea is the uncomfortable overlap between care and control. Does preserving someone’s memory honor them, or deny them the right to change—or disappear? I wouldn’t want a twist that resolves it. I’d want the final interaction to be small and difficult: deciding whether to correct a false account because it’s false, even though it’s the only account in which someone was loved.
